title: Minimum Time to Complete All Tasks
statement:
A computer can work on any number of tasks during the same second. Each entry `tasks[i] = [start_i, end_i, duration_i]` describes a task that must receive `duration_i` seconds of running time in total, all of them whole seconds inside the inclusive window `[start_i, end_i]`; those seconds do not have to be consecutive.

The computer may be switched on and off as often as you like, and while it is on it can run every task whose window contains the current second. Return the smallest number of seconds the computer has to be on so that every task gets its full duration.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every on/off pattern of the seconds is exponential. The greedy idea: handle tasks in order of their end time, and when a task still needs seconds, switch on the **latest** free seconds of its window. Every task handled later ends no earlier, so a late second lies inside as many of their windows as an earlier one would, and often more. Seconds already switched on are free to reuse, so each task first counts them.

## Approach

1. Sort `tasks` by `end`.
2. Keep `on`, one flag per second from 1 to 2000, and the count `total`.
3. For each task, set `need = duration` and subtract one for every second in `[start, end]` that is already on.
4. Walk `second` down from `end`, switching on seconds that are off, until `need` reaches 0, adding each to `total`.
5. Return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted by end: `[2,3,1]`, `[4,5,1]`, `[1,5,2]`. The first task finds nothing on in `[2,3]`, so second 3 is switched on. The second task finds nothing on in `[4,5]`, so second 5 is switched on. The third task already sees seconds 3 and 5 on inside `[1,5]`, so `need` drops to 0. `total = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n + n·T) with T = 2000: sorting, then each task scans its window at most twice.
- Space: O(T) for `on`.

## Pitfalls

- Sort by end time, not start time; otherwise a later-ending task may have used seconds an earlier deadline cannot reach.
- Count the seconds that are already on before switching on new ones, or shared seconds are paid for twice.
- Windows are inclusive at both ends.
- The backward walk never leaves the window, because `duration` is at most the window's length.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `on` | `on[second]` is true when the computer runs during that second |
| `total` | how many seconds are switched on so far |
| `start`, `end`, `duration` | the current task |
| `need` | seconds the current task still lacks |
| `second` | the time being examined |

narration.2: Process tasks by their deadline so later tasks can reuse the seconds chosen for earlier ones.
narration.3: One flag per second records whether the computer is on then.
narration.5: Take the tasks one at a time in order of end time.
narration.6: At first the task still needs its whole duration.
narration.7: Look at every second of its window...
narration.8: ...and count the ones already switched on, which this task gets for free.
narration.10: Fill the rest from the latest second of the window downward.
narration.11: A second that is still off can be switched on for this task.
narration.12: Switch it on; later tasks that end no earlier may reuse it.
narration.14: Count one more second of on time.
narration.18: Every task is satisfied; return how many seconds the computer was on.
